questions.stem: Plants have two types of transport tissue: xylem and phloem. A student says both transport systems work in the same way. Why is this incorrect?

options.text: Xylem and phloem carry the same substances
Xylem transports water and minerals upward (dead cells, one-way); phloem transports sugars both up and down (living cells, bidirectional)
Both are made of dead cells
Phloem only works at night

questions.explanation: Xylem and phloem differ significantly: xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes that transport water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves in one direction (driven by transpiration). Phloem sieve tubes are living cells that transport dissolved sugars (sucrose) from sources (leaves) to sinks (roots, fruits) in both directions (translocation).

questions.stem: In a cross-section of a young stem, xylem is typically found toward the inside and phloem toward the outside. A tree is girdled (a ring of bark including phloem is removed). What happens?

options.text: Water cannot reach the leaves, so the tree wilts immediately
Sugars cannot be transported to the roots, which eventually die, killing the tree
Nothing happens because xylem is unaffected
The tree grows faster because there is less resistance to water flow

questions.explanation: Girdling removes the phloem but leaves the xylem intact (as it is deeper in the stem). Water still reaches the leaves, so the tree does not wilt immediately. However, sugars produced in the leaves cannot be transported down to the roots through the destroyed phloem. The roots starve and die, eventually killing the entire tree.

questions.stem: Why do plants need a transport system even though they do not have a circulatory system like animals?

options.text: Plants are too small to need transport
Multicellular plants are too large for diffusion alone to supply all cells; transport tissues move water, minerals, and sugars efficiently over long distances
Plants only need transport during the day
Transport systems help plants move from place to place

questions.explanation: While single-celled organisms can rely on diffusion, multicellular plants have a large surface area to volume ratio challenge. Cells deep inside the plant are too far from the surface for diffusion to be fast enough. Xylem and phloem provide efficient long-distance transport of water (roots to leaves) and sugars (leaves to rest of plant).

questions.stem: A celery stalk is placed in water containing red food colouring. After several hours, red lines are visible inside the stalk. Which tissue has been stained?

options.text: Phloem, because it transports coloured substances
Xylem, because water and dissolved substances travel up through xylem vessels
Both xylem and phloem equally
The outer epidermis only

questions.explanation: The red food colouring dissolves in water and travels up through the xylem vessels by transpiration pull. This classic experiment demonstrates the pathway of water transport in plants. The red lines visible in the celery cross-section correspond to the position of the xylem vascular bundles.

questions.stem: In a root cross-section, the xylem is arranged in a star shape at the centre, while in a stem cross-section, xylem and phloem are arranged in vascular bundles around the edge. What is the advantage of the root arrangement?

options.text: The star shape in the root provides greater structural support against the pulling forces of anchorage and water uptake
The star shape allows the root to photosynthesise
There is no advantage; it is random
The central position helps xylem absorb more minerals

questions.explanation: The central, star-shaped arrangement of xylem in roots provides strength and rigidity at the core, helping the root resist the bending and pulling forces experienced as it anchors the plant in soil and absorbs water. In stems, the peripheral arrangement of vascular bundles provides resistance against bending forces from wind.
